title: Iterators with yield
body: An iterator method returns `IEnumerable<T>` (or `IEnumerator<T>`) and uses `yield return` to produce elements one at a time. The compiler turns the method into a state machine. Nothing in the body runs when you call the method; it runs piece by piece as the caller enumerates, pausing at each `yield return` and resuming on the next `MoveNext`.

`yield break` ends the sequence. Iterators can be infinite (`while (true) yield return next;`) because the caller decides how many elements to take. `finally` blocks in an iterator run when enumeration completes or when the `foreach` loop exits early and disposes the enumerator.

Because execution is deferred, argument validation inside an iterator also happens late: `ReadLines(null)` does not throw until the first `MoveNext`. The standard fix is a non-iterator public method that validates and then returns a call to a private (or local) iterator function.

Iterators cannot have `ref`, `out` or `in` parameters, and cannot `yield` inside a `catch` block. Since C# 13 they may contain `ref struct` locals and `unsafe` blocks as long as they do not cross a `yield`.
Check whether the caller may stop early (put cleanup in `finally`), whether validation should be eager, and whether enumerating twice re-runs side effects.

challenge: Write an iterator Primes() that yields primes forever using trial division, and print the first 10 with Take.
question: When does the body of an iterator method start running?
correct: On the first MoveNext call of an enumerator, not when the method is called
wrong: Immediately when the method is called
Only after the whole sequence has been requested
reasoning: Iterators are lazy state machines; that is why validation inside them is deferred too.
